<translation>
<pb n="28"/>In [that which is empty], how could it exist? If a self, purity, permanence, and happiness existed, then self, purity, permanence, and happiness would not be subversions. If a self, purity, permanence, and happiness do not exist, then selflessness, impurity, impermanence, and suffering do not exist either. Thus, by the ceasing of subversions, ignorance comes to cease. When ignorance has ceased, then karmic formations and the rest will cease. If some mental afflictions existed by their own nature, how could they ever be abandoned? Who can abandon what is inherently existent? If some mental afflictions did not exist by their own nature, how could they ever be abandoned? Who can abandon what is non-existent? This was the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Investigation of Subversions."

If all these things are empty, there would be no arising and no perishing. It would follow that for you, the four noble truths do not exist. Since the four noble truths would not exist, then thorough knowledge <note>of suffering</note>, abandonment <note>of the origin</note>, meditation <note>on the path</note>, and realization <note>of cessation</note> would not be tenable. Since those things would not exist, the four fruits <note>of the spiritual life: stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat</note> would also not exist. If the fruits do not exist, those who abide in the fruits do not exist, and those who enter the paths do not exist. If the eight types of persons <note>the four pairs of those entering and abiding in the four fruits</note> do not exist, then the Sangha <gloss>Spiritual Community</gloss> does not exist. Because the noble truths do not exist, the Sublime Dharma <gloss>Teachings</gloss> also does not exist. If the Dharma and the Sangha do not exist, how could a Buddha exist? By speaking thus of emptiness, you negate the Three Jewels, and you negate the existence of results, the nature of things that are not the Dharma, and all worldly conventions. To this we say: because you do not understand the purpose of emptiness, emptiness itself, and the meaning of emptiness, you are harmed by these views. The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas 

<pb n="29"/>is perfectly based upon two truths: the worldly relative truth <note>original: "samvrti-satya"</note> and the ultimate truth <note>original: "paramartha-satya"</note>. Those who do not understand the distinction between these two truths do not understand the profound reality of the Buddha's teaching. Without relying on convention, the ultimate cannot be taught. Without realizing the ultimate, nirvana <gloss>the state beyond suffering</gloss> cannot be attained. If emptiness is viewed wrongly, those of small wisdom will be ruined, just as a snake wrongly grasped or a secret mantra <gloss>ritual formula</gloss> wrongly performed causes harm. Therefore, knowing that the depth of this Dharma is difficult to fathom, the Sage's <note>the Buddha's</note> mind was at first turned away from teaching the Dharma. The faults you have attributed to emptiness are not applicable to the empty. Your rejection of emptiness does not apply to me. For whom emptiness is possible, everything is possible. For whom emptiness is not possible, nothing is possible. You are projecting your own faults onto me, like a person who, while actually riding a horse, forgets that he is on the horse. If you view entities as existing through their own nature, then you view entities as being without causes and conditions. You negate the result, the cause, the agent, the act, the object, arising, ceasing, and the fruit as well. That which is dependently originated is explained as emptiness. That is a dependent designation; it is the Middle Way itself. Because there is no phenomenon that is not dependently originated, there is no phenomenon that is not empty. If all this were not empty, there would be no arising and no perishing. It would follow that for you, the four noble truths do not exist. If things were not dependently originated, 

<pb n="30"/>how could suffering exist? It was said that suffering is impermanent; it does not exist in an inherent nature. If it existed by nature, how could it ever arise? Therefore, for one who negates emptiness, the origin <note>the second noble truth</note> cannot exist. If suffering existed by nature, cessation <note>the third noble truth</note> would not exist. Because you hold it to be naturally established, you negate cessation. If the path had an inherent nature, meditation would not be tenable. If that path is to be meditated upon, it cannot have an inherent nature for you. When suffering, origin, and cessation do not exist, what cessation of suffering do you expect to attain through the path? If one does not have thorough knowledge <note>of suffering</note> by its very nature, how could it ever be thoroughly known? Does its nature not remain? Likewise, abandonment, realization, meditation, and the four fruits are also untenable for you, just like thorough knowledge. How could one be able to attain a fruit that is not attained by its own nature through the grasping of an inherent nature? If the fruits do not exist, those who abide in the fruits do not exist, and those who enter the paths do not exist. If the eight types of persons do not exist, then the Sangha does not exist. Because the noble truths do not exist, the Sublime Dharma also does not exist. If the Dharma and the Sangha do not exist, how could a Buddha exist? For you, it follows that a Buddha would exist without depending on awakening. For you, it also follows that awakening would exist without depending on a Buddha. For you, one who is not a Buddha by their own nature would not attain awakening even if they strove in the conduct of awakening for the sake of awakening. No one would ever perform Dharma or non-Dharma actions. What could an un-empty thing do? In an inherent nature, there is no activity. 

<pb n="31"/>Even without Dharma and non-Dharma, a result would exist for you. For you, a result arising from the cause of Dharma and non-Dharma would not exist. If for you a result arises from the cause of Dharma and non-Dharma, why is the result arising from Dharma and non-Dharma not empty? Whoever negates the emptiness of dependent origination negates all worldly conventions. If one negates emptiness, there would be no activity whatsoever; an action would be a beginningless act, and a non-doer would be an agent. If inherent nature existed, all beings would be unproduced, unceasing, and would remain eternally, devoid of various states. If emptiness did not exist, there would be no attaining of what is not yet attained, no action to end suffering, and no abandoning of all mental afflictions. Whoever sees dependent origination sees suffering, the origin, cessation, and the path itself. This was the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Noble Truths."

If all these things are empty, there is no arising and no perishing. Through what abandoning or ceasing do you assert that nirvana occurs? If all these things are not empty, there is no arising and no perishing. Through what abandoning or ceasing do you assert that nirvana occurs? That which is without abandonment, without attainment, without annihilation, without permanence, without ceasing, and without arising—that is called nirvana. First of all, nirvana is not an entity; it would follow that it has the characteristics of aging and death. There is no entity that is without aging and death. If nirvana 

<pb n="32"/>were an entity, nirvana would be conditioned. There is no entity anywhere that is not conditioned. If nirvana were an entity, how could it be non-dependent? There is no entity anywhere that is not dependent. If nirvana were not an entity, how would it be a non-entity? Where nirvana is not an entity, it is not a non-entity either. If nirvana were not an entity, how could it be non-dependent? There is no non-entity that is not dependent. Whatever is the state of coming and going is dependent or caused; that which is not dependent and not caused is taught to be nirvana. The Teacher <note>the Buddha</note> said that arising and perishing are to be abandoned. Therefore, it is reasonable that nirvana is neither an entity nor a non-entity. If nirvana were both an entity and a non-entity, it would follow that it is both an entity and a non-existence, which is not reasonable. If nirvana were both an entity and a non-entity, nirvana would not be non-dependent, because those two are dependent. How could nirvana be both an entity and a non-entity? nirvana is unconditioned; entities and non-entities are conditioned. How could both an entity and a non-entity exist in nirvana? Those two do not exist in one place, like light and darkness. The teaching of nirvana as neither an entity nor a non-entity would be established if non-entities and entities were themselves established. If nirvana is neither an entity nor a non-entity, by what could "neither entity nor non-entity" be realized? When the Blessed One has entered nirvana, he is not perceived as "existing," 

<pb n="33"/>likewise not as "not existing," nor "both," nor "neither." Even when the Blessed One is present, he is not perceived as "existing," likewise not as "not existing," nor "both," nor "neither." There is not the slightest difference between cyclic existence <note>original: "samsara"</note> and nirvana. There is not the slightest difference between nirvana and cyclic existence. The limit of nirvana is the limit of cyclic existence; there is not even the subtlest difference between the two. Views concerning whether something exists after death, or that the world is permanent and so on, depend on nirvana, the future limit, and the prior limit. Since all things are empty, what is "finite," what is "infinite," what is "both finite and infinite," and what is "neither finite nor infinite"? What is "the same," what is "different," what is "permanent," what is "impermanent," what is "both permanent and impermanent," and what is "neither"? All perceptions are pacified, and all conceptual proliferations <note>original: "prapancha"</note> are pacified and peaceful. The Buddha never taught any Dharma to anyone, anywhere. This was the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Investigation of Nirvana."

Because of being obscured by ignorance, there is further existence; the three types of karmic formations are performed. By those karmic actions, one goes to the migrations. Consciousness, conditioned by karmic formations, enters the migrations. When consciousness has entered, name and form <note>the mental and physical components of a being</note> take shape. When name and form have taken shape, the six sense bases arise. Based on the six sense bases, contact arises. It is only arising based on name, form, and memory. Thus, based on name and form, 

<pb n="34"/>consciousness arises. The meeting of the three—eye, form, and consciousness—is contact. From that contact, feeling arises. Craving is conditioned by feeling; one craves for the sake of feeling. When there is craving, grasping occurs; the four types of grasping occur. When there is grasping, the existence of the grasper comes to be. If there is no grasping, one is liberated and existence does not occur. That existence is the five aggregates; from existence, birth arises. Aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental unease, and agitation all arise from birth. Thus, this whole mass of suffering arises. Karmic formations are the root of cyclic existence; therefore, the wise do not perform them. The unwise are the performers, because the wise see reality. When ignorance has ceased, karmic formations will not arise. The cessation of ignorance comes from meditating on reality with knowledge. Through the ceasing of this and that, this and that do not manifest. The whole mass of suffering thus completely ceases. This was the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Twelve Links of Existence."

Views such as whether one existed or did not exist in the past, or whether the world is permanent and so on, depend on the prior limit. Views such as whether one will exist or not exist in the future, or whether the world is finite and so on, depend on the future limit. The claim that one existed in the past is not tenable. That which existed in former times is not this very same one. If you think that that itself becomes the self, then 

<pb n="35"/>aside from grasping, what is your self? When a self does not exist aside from grasping, then if grasping itself were the self, your self would be non-existent. Grasping itself is not the self; it is that which arises and perishes. How can the object grasped be the grasper? It is not tenable for the self to be different from grasping. If it were different, it would be reasonable to perceive it without grasping, yet it is not perceived. Thus, it is not different from grasping, nor is it grasping itself. The self is not without grasping, but it is also not certain that it is non-existent. The claim that one did not exist in the past is also not tenable. This one is not different from the one who existed in former times. If this one were different, it would arise even without the other. Likewise, it would remain, and one would be born there without having died. It would follow that there would be annihilation, that actions would be wasted, and that actions performed by one would be experienced by another, and so forth. It does not arise from what has not existed, as this would be a fault. The self would be something created, or it would arise without a cause. Thus, the views concerning the past—that the self arose, did not arise, both, or neither—are not tenable. The views concerning whether one will exist or not exist in a future time are similar to those concerning the past. If that god were the same as this human, then he would be permanent. The god would be unproduced, because there is no birth for the permanent. If the human were different from the god, then he would be impermanent. If the god and the human were different, then a continuum would not be tenable. If one part were a god and one part were a human, it would be both permanent and impermanent. That too is not reasonable. If both permanence and impermanence were established, then "neither permanent nor impermanent" [would be established].
</translation>

<summary>This section of the Madhyamakakarika concludes the analysis of subversions and the Four Noble Truths, then moves into an investigation of nirvana, dependent origination, and views regarding the self in past and future lives. Nagarjuna argues that all phenomena, including the Buddha and nirvana, are empty of inherent nature and that understanding this emptiness is essential to the Middle Way.</summary>
<keywords>emptiness, four noble truths, two truths, nirvana, dependent origination, twelve links, samsara, self, permanence, impermanence</keywords>

If all this were not empty, there would be no arising and no perishing. It would follow that for you, the four noble truths do not exist. If things were not dependently originated,
pages.head: The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas

pages.span: how could suffering exist? It was said that suffering is impermanent; it does not exist in an inherent nature. If it existed by nature, how could it ever arise? Therefore, for one who negates emptiness, the origin <note>the second noble truth</note> cannot exist. If suffering existed by nature, cessation <note>the third noble truth</note> would not exist. Because you hold it to be naturally established, you negate cessation. If the path had an inherent nature, meditation would not be tenable. If that path is to be meditated upon, it cannot have an inherent nature for you. When suffering, origin, and cessation do not exist, what cessation of suffering do you expect to attain through the path? If one does not have thorough knowledge <note>of suffering</note> by its very nature, how could it ever be thoroughly known? Does its nature not remain? Likewise, abandonment, realization, meditation, and the four fruits are also untenable for you, just like thorough knowledge. How could one be able to attain a fruit that is not attained by its own nature through the grasping of an inherent nature? If the fruits do not exist, those who abide in the fruits do not exist, and those who enter the paths do not exist. If the eight types of persons do not exist, then the Sangha does not exist. Because the noble truths do not exist, the Sublime Dharma also does not exist. If the Dharma and the Sangha do not exist, how could a Buddha exist? For you, it follows that a Buddha would exist without depending on awakening. For you, it also follows that awakening would exist without depending on a Buddha. For you, one who is not a Buddha by their own nature would not attain awakening even if they strove in the conduct of awakening for the sake of awakening. No one would ever perform Dharma or non-Dharma actions. What could an un-empty thing do? In an inherent nature, there is no activity.
pages.head: If things were not dependently originated,

pages.span:
Even without Dharma and non-Dharma, a result would exist for you. For you, a result arising from the cause of Dharma and non-Dharma would not exist. If for you a result arises from the cause of Dharma and non-Dharma, why is the result arising from Dharma and non-Dharma not empty? Whoever negates the emptiness of dependent origination negates all worldly conventions. If one negates emptiness, there would be no activity whatsoever; an action would be a beginningless act, and a non-doer would be an agent. If inherent nature existed, all beings would be unproduced, unceasing, and would remain eternally, devoid of various states. If emptiness did not exist, there would be no attaining of what is not yet attained, no action to end suffering, and no abandoning of all mental afflictions. Whoever sees dependent origination sees suffering, the origin, cessation, and the path itself. This was the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Noble Truths."

If all these things are empty, there is no arising and no perishing. Through what abandoning or ceasing do you assert that nirvana occurs? If all these things are not empty, there is no arising and no perishing. Through what abandoning or ceasing do you assert that nirvana occurs? That which is without abandonment, without attainment, without annihilation, without permanence, without ceasing, and without arising—that is called nirvana. First of all, nirvana is not an entity; it would follow that it has the characteristics of aging and death. There is no entity that is without aging and death. If nirvana
pages.tail: were an entity, nirvana would be conditioned.

pages.span: were an entity, nirvana would be conditioned. There is no entity anywhere that is not conditioned. If nirvana were an entity, how could it be non-dependent? There is no entity anywhere that is not dependent. If nirvana were not an entity, how would it be a non-entity? Where nirvana is not an entity, it is not a non-entity either. If nirvana were not an entity, how could it be non-dependent? There is no non-entity that is not dependent. Whatever is the state of coming and going is dependent or caused; that which is not dependent and not caused is taught to be nirvana. The Teacher <note>the Buddha</note> said that arising and perishing are to be abandoned. Therefore, it is reasonable that nirvana is neither an entity nor a non-entity. If nirvana were both an entity and a non-entity, it would follow that it is both an entity and a non-existence, which is not reasonable. If nirvana were both an entity and a non-entity, nirvana would not be non-dependent, because those two are dependent. How could nirvana be both an entity and a non-entity? nirvana is unconditioned; entities and non-entities are conditioned. How could both an entity and a non-entity exist in nirvana? Those two do not exist in one place, like light and darkness. The teaching of nirvana as neither an entity nor a non-entity would be established if non-entities and entities were themselves established. If nirvana is neither an entity nor a non-entity, by what could "neither entity nor non-entity" be realized? When the Blessed One has entered nirvana, he is not perceived as "existing,"
pages.head: If nirvana
pages.tail: likewise not as "not existing," nor "both," nor "neither."

pages.span:
likewise not as "not existing," nor "both," nor "neither." Even when the Blessed One is present, he is not perceived as "existing," likewise not as "not existing," nor "both," nor "neither." There is not the slightest difference between cyclic existence <note>original: "samsara"</note> and nirvana. There is not the slightest difference between nirvana and cyclic existence. The limit of nirvana is the limit of cyclic existence; there is not even the subtlest difference between the two. Views concerning whether something exists after death, or that the world is permanent and so on, depend on nirvana, the future limit, and the prior limit. Since all things are empty, what is "finite," what is "infinite," what is "both finite and infinite," and what is "neither finite nor infinite"? What is "the same," what is "different," what is "permanent," what is "impermanent," what is "both permanent and impermanent," and what is "neither"? All perceptions are pacified, and all conceptual proliferations <note>original: "prapancha"</note> are pacified and peaceful. The Buddha never taught any Dharma to anyone, anywhere. This was the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Investigation of Nirvana."

Because of being obscured by ignorance, there is further existence; the three types of karmic formations are performed. By those karmic actions, one goes to the migrations. Consciousness, conditioned by karmic formations, enters the migrations. When consciousness has entered, name and form <note>the mental and physical components of a being</note> take shape. When name and form have taken shape, the six sense bases arise. Based on the six sense bases, contact arises. It is only arising based on name, form, and memory. Thus, based on name and form,
pages.head: When the Blessed One has entered nirvana, he is not perceived as "existing,"

pages.span:
consciousness arises. The meeting of the three—eye, form, and consciousness—is contact. From that contact, feeling arises. Craving is conditioned by feeling; one craves for the sake of feeling. When there is craving, grasping occurs; the four types of grasping occur. When there is grasping, the existence of the grasper comes to be. If there is no grasping, one is liberated and existence does not occur. That existence is the five aggregates; from existence, birth arises. Aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental unease, and agitation all arise from birth. Thus, this whole mass of suffering arises. Karmic formations are the root of cyclic existence; therefore, the wise do not perform them. The unwise are the performers, because the wise see reality. When ignorance has ceased, karmic formations will not arise. The cessation of ignorance comes from meditating on reality with knowledge. Through the ceasing of this and that, this and that do not manifest. The whole mass of suffering thus completely ceases. This was the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Investigation of the Twelve Links of Existence."

Views such as whether one existed or did not exist in the past, or whether the world is permanent and so on, depend on the prior limit. Views such as whether one will exist or not exist in the future, or whether the world is finite and so on, depend on the future limit. The claim that one existed in the past is not tenable. That which existed in former times is not this very same one. If you think that that itself becomes the self, then
pages.head: Thus, based on name and form,
pages.tail: aside from grasping, what is your self?

pages.span: aside from grasping, what is your self? When a self does not exist aside from grasping, then if grasping itself were the self, your self would be non-existent. Grasping itself is not the self; it is that which arises and perishes. How can the object grasped be the grasper? It is not tenable for the self to be different from grasping. If it were different, it would be reasonable to perceive it without grasping, yet it is not perceived. Thus, it is not different from grasping, nor is it grasping itself. The self is not without grasping, but it is also not certain that it is non-existent. The claim that one did not exist in the past is also not tenable. This one is not different from the one who existed in former times. If this one were different, it would arise even without the other. Likewise, it would remain, and one would be born there without having died. It would follow that there would be annihilation, that actions would be wasted, and that actions performed by one would be experienced by another, and so forth. It does not arise from what has not existed, as this would be a fault. The self would be something created, or it would arise without a cause. Thus, the views concerning the past—that the self arose, did not arise, both, or neither—are not tenable. The views concerning whether one will exist or not exist in a future time are similar to those concerning the past. If that god were the same as this human, then he would be permanent. The god would be unproduced, because there is no birth for the permanent. If the human were different from the god, then he would be impermanent. If the god and the human were different, then a continuum would not be tenable. If one part were a god and one part were a human, it would be both permanent and impermanent. That too is not reasonable. If both permanence and impermanence were established, then "neither permanent nor impermanent" [would be established].
